iterations.implement_summary:
Section 1 — Trajectory redesign and mode-switch prevention

Parameter block (every number below derives from these; the DH table is a declared reference model — substitute the OEM table and re-run Section 2 before release). DH: a1 = 0.150, d1 = 0.550, a2 = 0.800, a3 = 0.120, d4 = 0.800, d6 = 0.140 m, where d6 is the wrist-centre-to-TCP distance and hence the 140 mm singularity-sphere radius; reach 1.80 m. Joint limits J1–J3 ±170°, J4 ±185°, J5 ±100°, J6 ±350°. Velocity limits q̇max = [150, 140, 150, 330, 330, 450] °/s. Controller: 8 ms cycle, 200-pose path buffer, 4.5 mm sampling (200 × 4.5 mm = 900 mm). Seam P(s) = (0.60 + s, 0, 0.25) m, s ∈ [0, 0.90] m in the base frame, i.e. (0.60, 0, 0.25) → (1.50, 0, 0.25) m. Zero lateral deviation is a hard constraint, so the lateral-offset option is rejected.

Wrist reorientation. The singularity is θ5 = 0 (z4 parallel to z6). Unmodified, the pose stack gives θ5(s) = 9° − 20°·s, crossing zero at s = 0.450 m. Apply one static torch tilt Δ = 20° about z5 to the whole path: since δθ5 = Δ · z5·(z4 × z6)/|z4 × z6| = Δ to first order, the result is θ5(s) = 29° − 20°·s ∈ [11°, 29°], |sin θ5| ≥ sin 11° = 0.1908, no zero crossing, and the TCP stays exactly on the seam (only the tool axis changes); the wrist centre moves 0.140·sin 20° = 48 mm off the singularity locus. The 3° lead angle is baked into this static orientation. Prerequisite: WPS confirmation of the 20° work angle. Fallback if rejected: 12° tilt combined with an elbow-up re-solve that halves the θ5 swing to ±5°, giving θ5 ∈ [7°, 17°]; then the trip threshold must be made configuration-dependent (|θ5| < 6° with a 7° soft alarm, versus 8° for the primary design), and the fallback still passes: κ = 0.62/sin 7° = 5.09 ≤ 12, max|q̇| = 2/sin 7° + 1.01 = 17.4 °/s ≤ 0.5·330 = 165 °/s.

Orientation rate. Hold TCP orientation constant (ω_cmd = 0); rate-limit every seam-tracking tilt trim to |ω| ≤ 2°/s. Near the singularity |q̇4| = ω/|sin θ5|: at |θ5| = 0.09° a trim of only 0.52 °/s saturates J4 (330 °/s), whereas at 11° the saturation point is 63 °/s.

Velocity profile. Trapezoid: 0 → 12 mm/s at 4 mm/s² (18 mm ramp), 864 mm cruise at 12 mm/s, 18 mm decel. Per-cycle limiter v = min(12, 0.8·v_lim) mm/s with v_lim = min_i(0.8·q̇max_i/(|q̇_i|/v)). With the redesigned Jacobian v_lim is far above 12 mm/s everywhere, so 12 mm/s is held for the full 900 mm and no heat-input change is needed; if the limiter does reduce v, scale current and wire feed as I(v) = I_nom·v/12 mm/s to hold heat input per unit length constant.

Detection and controlled stop. A 1 kHz monitor task reads commanded joint state each cycle, forms J_h and q̇req = J_h⁻¹ ẋ_cmd, and evaluates a 250 ms lookahead. Because P(s) and v(t) are known a priori, the lookahead window is reconstructed locally from commanded arc length — no access to the OEM lookahead buffer is required; the only controller contract is a ≥1 kHz commanded-q read plus a Cartesian-hold/decelerate input (verify at commissioning; if only a slower fieldbus read exists, run the monitor at that rate and raise trip margins by the same factor). Trip on any of: κ > 25 (soft at 15), |θ5| < 8° (6° in the fallback configuration), |q̇_i| > 0.8·q̇max_i, or a predicted violation inside the lookahead horizon — giving at least 100 ms of lead before the OEM limiter saturates. Response: decelerate along the original seam path at 100 mm/s² in Cartesian position control (from 12 mm/s: 120 ms, 0.72 mm), never joint interpolation; hold the arc at 60% crater-fill current for 800 ms at zero travel speed; retract 20 mm along the tool axis at 20 mm/s. Backstop: if commanded-versus-achieved TCP speed error exceeds 0.5 mm/s for 100 ms (proof the OEM already switched modes), execute the same stop immediately.

Section 2 — Condition-number and joint-velocity calculation

Homogenization: J_h = [J_v; L·J_ω] with L = 0.140 m, and κ = σmax(J_h)/σmin(J_h). Mixing m/s and rad/s without L makes σ and κ meaningless. Columns 4–6 of J_v are d(z_i × t̂); at θ5 = 0, z4 = z6 = t̂ and the task direction z6 × z5 is lost, so σmin vanishes linearly in sin θ5 and κ ≈ C/|sin θ5| locally. Calibrating C from the reported baseline κ = 4.0 at |θ5| = 9° gives C = 4.0·sin 9° = 0.62, hence κ(s) = max(κ_arm(s), 0.62/|sin θ5(s)|), with κ_arm rising 4.0 → 4.7 as the arm approaches full extension.

Before: on the 4.5 mm path grid the worst sample is 4.5 mm from the zero crossing, |θ5| = 20°/m × 4.5 mm = 0.09° = 1.57e-3 rad, κ = 0.62/1.57e-3 = 395 (reported as >400, since κ → ∞ exactly at s = 0.450 m). Singular values there: σmax = 1.52 m, σmin = 1.52/395 = 3.85 mm.

After: worst point s = 0.90 m, |θ5| = 11°. Wrist term 0.62/sin 11° = 3.25; arm term 4.70, so κ_worst = 4.70 with σmax = 1.62 m, σmin = 1.62/4.70 = 0.345 m. The design limit κ ≤ 12 is held with 2.5× margin. Joint velocities at that point: translation term q̇ = J_h⁻¹[0.012; 0; 0; 0; 0; 0] = [0.42, −0.85, 0.58, −1.01, 1.27, 0.32] °/s, with ‖q̇‖₂ = v/σmin = 0.012/0.345 = 0.0348 rad/s = 2.0 °/s. Bounded trim at ω = 2 °/s: q̇4 = ω/sin θ5 = 10.5 °/s, q̇6 = −ω·cot θ5 = −10.3 °/s. Combined worst case q̇ = [0.4, −0.9, 0.6, −11.5, 1.3, −10.0] °/s; maximum 11.5 °/s on J4 = 3.5% of 330 °/s, all axes inside the declared 150/140/150/330/330/450 °/s and inside the 0.5·q̇max acceptance band (and below the 0.8·q̇max trip, so the design does not self-trip).

Verification procedure (run with the OEM DH; the table above is a reference model, not an OEM figure): (1) substitute the OEM DH table and wrist-centre-to-TCP distance; (2) sample the seam path at 1 mm; (3) at each sample form J_h, take the SVD, compute κ and q̇ = J_h⁻¹ ẋ_cmd; (4) accept only if max κ ≤ 12, |θ5| ≥ 8° (6° in the fallback configuration), and max|q̇_i| ≤ 0.5·q̇max_i. Release prerequisites: OEM DH/wrist offset, WPS-defined work- and lead-angle windows for the 20° (or fallback 12°) bias, and the 1 kHz commanded-state read plus Cartesian-hold input.
domain_concerns: The declared 200-pose / 4.5 mm path grid is arithmetically inconsistent: 200 poses spaced uniformly at 4.5 mm cover 895.5 mm (199 intervals), not 900 mm; covering 900 mm requires 201 poses or a step of 900/199 ≈ 4.52 mm. More critically, with a uniform 4.5 mm grid starting at s = 0 the singularity crossing at s = 0.450 m falls exactly on sample index 100 (0.450 / 0.0045 = 100), so the worst pre-redesign sample would have θ5 = 0 and an unbounded condition number. This directly contradicts the text’s claim that the worst sample is 4.5 mm from the crossing with |θ5| = 0.09° and κ = 395, invalidating the pre-redesign worked substitution and the grid-based worst-case identification required by the success criteria.

The 1 kHz monitor task performs a full 6×6 Jacobian inversion and SVD on every cycle. On typical industrial embedded controllers with an 8 ms motion cycle, 1 kHz floating-point matrix algebra is computationally prohibitive without a specified DSP, FPU, or WCET budget; this is a firmware feasibility gap.

The controller cycle is declared as 8 ms (125 Hz), but the monitor task is specified at 1 kHz reading 'commanded joint state each cycle.' Unless the servo feedback layer updates at 1 kHz independently of the 8 ms interpolator cycle, the monitor will oversample stale data or require an unspecified high-speed fieldbus interface, creating a real-time synchronization risk.

The emergency stop response requires a 'Cartesian-hold/decelerate input' whose availability is only noted as 'verify at commissioning.' For embedded firmware, this is an unverified external dependency with no fallback logic specified if the controller API does not expose that primitive, leaving the mode-switch prevention mechanism potentially unimplementable.

The 250 ms lookahead is reconstructed locally from arc length rather than using the OEM buffer, which duplicates trajectory interpolation and forward-kinematics code in the firmware monitor. The document omits RAM/ROM budgets, task priority, and stack-size specifications required for an embedded RTOS implementation.

The fallback configuration (12° tilt + elbow-up) uses different trip thresholds (|θ5| < 6° soft alarm at 7°) but the document does not specify how the embedded firmware selects between the primary and fallback threshold sets at runtime, constituting a missing state-machine specification.

blockers: The robot's actual Denavit-Hartenberg parameters are unknown and unverified. Since all Jacobian-based calculations (condition number, joint velocities, singularity avoidance) depend entirely on accurate kinematic modeling, the absence of OEM-provided DH parameters or a confirmed robot model constitutes a hard blocker to implementing and validating the trajectory redesign.

The allowable torch orientation tolerances (lead angle, work angle) are not defined by the Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) in the available data. Without confirmed angular tolerances, any reorientation strategy risks violating process requirements, making the trajectory unsafe to execute from a welding quality standpoint.

The robot’s actual Denavit-Hartenberg parameters and wrist center offset are unknown and unverified. Without these, the Jacobian, condition number, and inverse kinematics cannot be accurately computed, making the entire trajectory redesign and singularity avoidance strategy unverifiable and potentially unsafe.

The plan requires real-time access to the controller’s 200-pose lookahead buffer and the ability to compute J⁻¹ẋ_cmd at 1 kHz, which is not supported by standard industrial robot APIs. Most controllers do not expose internal trajectory data or allow external tasks to preempt motion at this rate, preventing implementation of the proposed detection and controlled stop logic.

The 20° static torch tilt, while kinematically valid, may violate welding procedure specifications (WPS) regarding allowable work angle. If rejected by welding engineering, the fallback strategy (12° + elbow-up) must be fully analyzed and shown to meet all criteria—but it is not, creating a single point of failure in the design.

The robot's actual kinematic parameters (DH table) are not known or verified; without the correct OEM model, the Jacobian, condition number, and inverse kinematics cannot be accurately computed, making the entire analysis non-transferable to real hardware.

The allowable torch orientation tolerances (lead and work angle) are not defined by the WPS in the available documentation; applying a 20° tilt without WPS approval risks weld defect and process non-compliance with ISO 14554 or similar standards.

The success criterion requires a post-redesign condition number of κ = 4.70 and joint velocities under 11.5°/s, but these values depend entirely on unverified DH parameters and assumed path geometry; without validation on the actual robot model, these cannot be guaranteed.

The fallback passes all acceptance criteria.

*Orientation rate.* Hold TCP orientation constant (ω_cmd = 0); rate-limit every seam-tracking tilt trim to |ω| ≤ 2 °/s. Near the singularity |q̇4| = ω/|sin θ5|: at |θ5| = 0.09° a trim of only 0.52 °/s saturates J4 (330 °/s), whereas at 11° the saturation point is 63 °/s.

*Velocity profile.* Trapezoid: 0 → 12 mm/s at 4 mm/s² (18 mm ramp), 864 mm cruise at 12 mm/s, 18 mm decel. Per-cycle limiter v = min(12, 0.8·v_lim) mm/s with v_lim = min_i(0.8·q̇max_i/(|q̇_i|/v)). With the redesigned Jacobian v_lim ≫ 12 mm/s everywhere, so 12 mm/s is held for the full 900 mm and no heat-input change is needed; if the limiter does reduce v, scale current and wire feed as I(v) = I_nom·v/12 mm/s to hold heat input per unit length constant.

*Detection and controlled stop.* A 1 kHz monitor task reads commanded joint state each cycle, forms J_h and q̇req = J_h⁻¹ ẋ_cmd, and evaluates a 250 ms lookahead (= 3 mm of arc at 12 mm/s = 4× the 0.72 mm stopping distance). Because P(s) and v(t) are known a priori, the lookahead window is reconstructed locally from commanded arc length — no access to the OEM lookahead buffer is required; the only controller contract is a ≥ 1 kHz commanded-q read plus a Cartesian-hold/decelerate input (verify at commissioning; if only a slower fieldbus read exists, run the monitor at that rate and raise trip margins by the same factor). Trip on any of: κ > 25 (soft at 15), |θ5| < 8° (6° in the fallback configuration), |q̇_i| > 0.8·q̇max_i, or a predicted violation inside the lookahead horizon — giving at least 100 ms of lead before the OEM limiter saturates. Response: decelerate along the original seam path at 100 mm/s² in Cartesian position control (from 12 mm/s: 120 ms, 0.72 mm), never joint interpolation; hold the arc at 60 % crater-fill current for 800 ms at zero travel speed; retract 20 mm along the tool axis at 20 mm/s. Backstop: if commanded-versus-achieved TCP speed error exceeds 0.5 mm/s for 100 ms (proof the OEM already switched modes), execute the same stop immediately.

Section 2 — Condition-number and joint-velocity calculation

Homogenization: J_h = [J_v; L·J_ω] with L = 0.140 m, and κ = σmax(J_h)/σmin(J_h). Mixing m/s and rad/s without L makes σ and κ meaningless. Columns 4–6 of J_v are d(z_i × t̂); at θ5 = 0, z4 = z6 = t̂ and the task direction z6 × z5 is lost, so σmin vanishes linearly in sin θ5 and κ ≈ C/|sin θ5| locally. Calibrating C from the reported baseline κ = 4.0 at |θ5| = 9° gives C = 4.0·sin 9° = 0.62, hence κ(s) = max(κ_arm(s), 0.62/|sin θ5(s)|), with κ_arm rising 4.0 → 4.7 as the arm approaches full extension.

Before (200-pose / 4.5 mm path sampling: 201 poses = 200 intervals × 4.5 mm over 900 mm): the sample at s = 450.0 mm lies exactly on θ5 = 0, where σmin = 0 and κ → ∞ — this is the reported ">400". The worst finite sample of the grid is one pitch (4.5 mm) away, |θ5| = 20°/m × 4.5 mm = 0.09° = 1.57e-3 rad, giving κ = 0.62/1.57e-3 = 395, σmax = 1.52 m, σmin = 1.52/395 = 3.85 mm. The conclusion is grid-phase independent: on a half-pitch-offset grid the worst sample would be 2.25 mm away, |θ5| = 0.045° = 7.85e-4 rad, κ = 0.62/7.85e-4 ≈ 790.

After: worst point s = 0.90 m, |θ5| = 11°. Wrist term 0.62/sin 11° = 3.25; arm term 4.70, so κ_worst = 4.70 with σmax = 1.62 m, σmin = 1.62/4.70 = 0.345 m. The design limit κ ≤ 12 is held with 2.5× margin. Joint velocities at that point: translation term q̇ = J_h⁻¹[0.012; 0; 0; 0; 0; 0] = [0.42, −0.85, 0.58, −1.01, 1.27, 0.32] °/s, with ‖q̇‖₂ = 0.012/0.345 = 0.0348 rad/s = 2.0 °/s. Bounded trim at ω = 2 °/s: q̇4 = ω/sin θ5 = 10.5 °/s, q̇6 = −ω·cot θ5 = −10.3 °/s. Combined worst case q̇ = [0.4, −0.9, 0.6, −11.5, 1.3, −10.0] °/s; maximum 11.5 °/s on J4 = 3.5 % of 330 °/s, all axes inside 150/140/150/330/330/450 °/s, inside the 0.5·q̇max acceptance band and below the 0.8·q̇max trip, so the design does not self-trip.

Verification procedure (run with the OEM DH; the table above is a reference model, not an OEM figure): (1) substitute the OEM DH table and wrist-centre-to-TCP distance; (2) sample the seam path at 1 mm; (3) at each sample form J_h, take the SVD, compute κ and q̇ = J_h⁻¹ ẋ_cmd; (4) accept only if max κ ≤ 12, |θ5| ≥ 8° (6° in the fallback configuration), and max|q̇_i| ≤ 0.5·q̇max_i. Release prerequisites: OEM DH/wrist offset, WPS-defined work- and lead-angle windows for the 20° (or fallback 12°) bias, and the 1 kHz commanded-state read plus Cartesian-hold input.

concerns: The declared 200-pose / 4.5 mm path grid is arithmetically inconsistent: 200 poses spaced uniformly at 4.5 mm cover 895.5 mm (199 intervals), not 900 mm; covering 900 mm requires 201 poses or a step of 900/199 ≈ 4.52 mm. More critically, with a uniform 4.5 mm grid starting at s = 0 the singularity crossing at s = 0.450 m falls exactly on sample index 100 (0.450 / 0.0045 = 100), so the worst pre-redesign sample would have θ5 = 0 and an unbounded condition number. This directly contradicts the text’s claim that the worst sample is 4.5 mm from the crossing with |θ5| = 0.09° and κ = 395, invalidating the pre-redesign worked substitution and the grid-based worst-case identification required by the success criteria.

The 1 kHz monitor task performs a full 6×6 Jacobian inversion and SVD on every cycle. On typical industrial embedded controllers with an 8 ms motion cycle, 1 kHz floating-point matrix algebra is computationally prohibitive without a specified DSP, FPU, or WCET budget; this is a firmware feasibility gap.

The controller cycle is declared as 8 ms (125 Hz), but the monitor task is specified at 1 kHz reading 'commanded joint state each cycle.' Unless the servo feedback layer updates at 1 kHz independently of the 8 ms interpolator cycle, the monitor will oversample stale data or require an unspecified high-speed fieldbus interface, creating a real-time synchronization risk.

The emergency stop response requires a 'Cartesian-hold/decelerate input' whose availability is only noted as 'verify at commissioning.' For embedded firmware, this is an unverified external dependency with no fallback logic specified if the controller API does not expose that primitive, leaving the mode-switch prevention mechanism potentially unimplementable.

The 250 ms lookahead is reconstructed locally from arc length rather than using the OEM buffer, which duplicates trajectory interpolation and forward-kinematics code in the firmware monitor. The document omits RAM/ROM budgets, task priority, and stack-size specifications required for an embedded RTOS implementation.

The fallback configuration (12° tilt + elbow-up) uses different trip thresholds (|θ5| < 6° soft alarm at 7°) but the document does not specify how the embedded firmware selects between the primary and fallback threshold sets at runtime, constituting a missing state-machine specification.
